label: Stop 1: The trains over Wabash Avenue

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay. I'm walking south and there's a giant steel thing over my head.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: That's the elevated track for the L, Chicago's elevated train.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Stand under it for a moment, and listen when a train goes over.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Loud.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Yes. It always has been. Chicago's first L train ran on June 6, 1892, from Thirty-ninth Street and State Street to Congress Parkway and Wabash Avenue.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Why put trains in the air at all?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Because the streets were choked.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Horse-drawn streetcars, and then cable cars, couldn't carry the crowds as the city grew, and the cars added to the congestion.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So they went up.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A businessman named Charles Yerkes built elevated tracks above downtown streets to connect the separate lines.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: That's the Loop. The first full circuit of it was finished in 1897.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Why's it called the Loop?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The name is said to come from the cable cars that once looped around several downtown blocks.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Then it stuck to the whole downtown.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So when people say "the Loop," they mean the area, and the tracks, and the cable cars?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: All three. Now look at the steel.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was designed by the bridge designer John Alexander Low Waddell, and it's riveted steel plate.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: One architecture guide says it resembles the Eiffel Tower and the first Ferris wheel, which were built just before.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: An elevated railroad that looks like the Eiffel Tower.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A little. And it's still working after more than a century.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Since 1993 the lines have color names, but the old structure is the same.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay, that's cool. A bit. Don't tell Ben I said cool.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: I'm Ben.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Right. Don't tell yourself.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Keep walking south on Wabash. The pub is just ahead, beside the tracks.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: About a four-minute walk.
